about: Original demo question bank for the StudyBuddy public demo. Every evidence_quote must appear verbatim in demo/corpus or the importer drops the question.

concepts.name: Linear regression
concepts.description: Predicting a continuous target as a weighted sum of features plus an intercept, fitted by minimising squared error.
key_facts: Regression predicts a real value, classification predicts a category
Each weight is the change in prediction per unit of its feature with others held fixed
Residual = true target minus prediction
Sensitive to outliers because large residuals are squared

questions.question: What separates a regression problem from a classification problem?
options: Classification always uses mean squared error
Regression needs labelled data; classification does not
Regression outputs a real value; classification outputs a category
Regression can only use one input feature
questions.correct_answer: Regression outputs a real value; classification outputs a category
questions.explanation: Linear regression predicts a continuous number such as a price or a mark. Classification predicts which category an example belongs to.
questions.evidence_quote: The output is a real value, not a category, which is what separates regression from classification.

questions.question: In a multi-feature linear regression model, what does a single weight tell you?
options: The prediction when every feature is zero
The probability that the feature is relevant
The average value of that feature in the training set
How much the prediction changes when that feature rises by one unit, with other features held fixed
questions.correct_answer: How much the prediction changes when that feature rises by one unit, with other features held fixed
questions.explanation: A weight is a per-unit effect of its feature on the prediction, holding the others constant. The prediction at all-zero features is the intercept, not a weight.
questions.evidence_quote: Each weight says how much the prediction changes when that feature increases by one unit and every other feature is held fixed.

questions.question: You plot residuals against predictions and see them fan out as predictions grow. What does that suggest?
options: The model is a perfect fit
The noise is not constant across the range, so a plain linear model may be a poor fit
There are too few features to compute residuals
The learning rate was too high
questions.correct_answer: The noise is not constant across the range, so a plain linear model may be a poor fit
questions.explanation: Residuals that look like random noise around zero support a linear model. A curve or a fan shape points to non-linearity or non-constant noise.
questions.evidence_quote: If they curve or fan out, the relationship is probably not linear, or the noise is not constant across the range.

questions.question: Why is linear regression fitted with mean squared error sensitive to outliers?
questions.correct_answer: Because the residuals are squared, a single large residual from an outlier grows much bigger and dominates the loss.
questions.explanation: Squaring magnifies large errors, so one outlier can pull the fitted line towards itself.
questions.evidence_quote: It is sensitive to outliers, because squaring a large residual makes it dominate the loss.

concepts.name: Loss functions and least squares
concepts.description: How a loss function scores model error, the difference between MSE and MAE, and when to use the normal equation versus gradient descent.
key_facts: MSE squares residuals and punishes large errors heavily
MAE grows linearly so it is less sensitive to outliers
The normal equation is a closed-form solution for least squares
Report loss on a held-out test set to estimate real performance

questions.question: Why is mean absolute error less sensitive to outliers than mean squared error?
options: Its gradient is always zero near outliers
It is computed only on the test set
It grows linearly with the error instead of quadratically
It ignores any residual larger than one
questions.correct_answer: It grows linearly with the error instead of quadratically
questions.explanation: An outlier's error is added as-is under MAE, but squared under MSE, so it carries far less weight under MAE.
questions.evidence_quote: Because it grows linearly rather than quadratically, it is far less sensitive to outliers than mean squared error.

questions.question: When does the normal equation become a poor choice for fitting linear regression?
options: When the loss is mean squared error
When there are many thousands of features, because it inverts a matrix that grows with the feature count
When the dataset has fewer than 100 rows
When the features have been standardised
questions.correct_answer: When there are many thousands of features, because it inverts a matrix that grows with the feature count
questions.explanation: The closed-form solution needs a matrix inversion whose cost grows quickly with the number of features. Gradient descent scales better there.
questions.evidence_quote: so it becomes slow when there are many thousands of features. In that case an iterative method such as gradient descent is the usual choice

questions.question: A model has very low training loss and much higher test loss. What is the most likely explanation?
options: It is underfitting
The loss function is not differentiable
It is memorising the training data rather than learning the pattern
The test set is too large
questions.correct_answer: It is memorising the training data rather than learning the pattern
questions.explanation: A large gap between training and test loss is the classic sign of memorisation, which the next topics call overfitting.
questions.evidence_quote: A model with a very low training loss and a much higher test loss is memorising rather than learning.

questions.question: What does a loss function do in model training?
questions.correct_answer: It turns how wrong the model is into a single number, and training searches for the parameters that minimise the average loss.
questions.explanation: Defining a loss turns learning into an optimisation problem.
questions.evidence_quote: A loss function turns "how wrong is the model" into a single number that training can minimise.

concepts.name: Gradient descent
concepts.description: Iteratively stepping parameters against the gradient of the loss; batch, stochastic and mini-batch variants; convergence behaviour.
key_facts: Move parameters in the opposite direction of the gradient
Step size is the gradient times the learning rate
Mini-batch uses a small random subset, often 32 to 256 examples
Convex losses have a single global minimum

questions.question: In which direction does gradient descent move the parameters?
options: Along the gradient of the loss
Towards the largest parameter
Perpendicular to the gradient
Opposite to the gradient of the loss
questions.correct_answer: Opposite to the gradient of the loss
questions.explanation: The gradient points uphill, towards steepest increase. To reduce the loss you step the other way.
questions.evidence_quote: Gradient descent therefore moves the parameters in the opposite direction of the gradient.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off of stochastic gradient descent compared with batch gradient descent?
options: It always converges to a worse minimum
Each step is cheap, but the path is noisy
It cannot be used with mean squared error
Each step is exact, but very expensive
questions.correct_answer: Each step is cheap, but the path is noisy
questions.explanation: Updating after one example costs little per step, but a single example gives a rough estimate of the true gradient.
questions.evidence_quote: Stochastic gradient descent updates the parameters after every single example, which is cheap per step but makes the path noisy.

questions.question: Why is gradient descent guaranteed to reach the global minimum for linear regression with mean squared error (given a suitable learning rate)?
options: Linear regression has no parameters to learn
Mean squared error is always zero at the start
The loss is convex, so there is only one minimum
The gradient is constant everywhere
questions.correct_answer: The loss is convex, so there is only one minimum
questions.explanation: A convex loss has no local minima other than the global one, so going downhill always ends in the right place.
questions.evidence_quote: For a convex loss such as mean squared error in linear regression, there is only one minimum

questions.question: How can the noise in mini-batch gradient estimates actually help training?
questions.correct_answer: Random variation in the gradient can push the parameters out of shallow local minima and saddle points.
questions.explanation: An exact gradient can get stuck where the surface is flat; noise can knock the parameters free.
questions.evidence_quote: Random variation in the gradient can push the parameters out of shallow local minima and saddle points

concepts.name: Learning rate and feature scaling
concepts.description: Picking a learning rate, reading loss curves, learning rate schedules, and why scaling features speeds up gradient descent.
key_facts: Too small a learning rate is slow; too large overshoots or diverges
A zigzagging or rising loss curve suggests the learning rate is too high
Unscaled features make a long narrow valley that slows gradient descent
Fit scaling statistics on the training set only

questions.question: Your training loss zigzags and then starts climbing. What is the most likely cause?
options: The learning rate is too low
The model has too few epochs
The features are already standardised
The learning rate is too high
questions.correct_answer: The learning rate is too high
questions.explanation: Overly large steps overshoot the minimum, so the loss bounces around or grows.
questions.evidence_quote: A curve that zigzags or climbs suggests the learning rate is too high.

questions.question: Why do many training runs reduce the learning rate over time?
options: It removes the need for a validation set
Large early steps cover ground quickly, and smaller later steps let the parameters settle into the minimum
A smaller learning rate always reaches a better minimum from the very start
The gradient grows over time, so the rate must shrink to keep steps the same
questions.correct_answer: Large early steps cover ground quickly, and smaller later steps let the parameters settle into the minimum
questions.explanation: A schedule gets the speed of big steps early and the precision of small steps late.
questions.evidence_quote: Large early steps cover ground quickly, and smaller later steps let the parameters settle into the minimum instead of jumping around it.

questions.question: When standardising features, where should the mean and standard deviation be computed?
options: Separately on each set
On the test set, because it represents new data
On the full dataset including the test set
On the training set only, then applied to validation and test sets
questions.correct_answer: On the training set only, then applied to validation and test sets
questions.explanation: Using test data to compute scaling statistics leaks information about the test set into training.
questions.evidence_quote: compute the scaling statistics on the training set only and then apply the same transformation to the validation and test sets

questions.question: Why does feature scaling speed up gradient descent?
questions.correct_answer: Features with very different ranges make the loss surface a long narrow valley, so gradient descent zigzags. Scaling makes the valley rounder so it can head more directly to the minimum.
questions.explanation: Similar feature ranges give a better-conditioned loss surface.
questions.evidence_quote: Rescaling the features to similar ranges makes the valley rounder, so gradient descent can head more directly to the minimum.

concepts.name: Overfitting and the bias-variance trade-off
concepts.description: Underfitting versus overfitting, bias and variance as sources of error, and diagnosing which problem a model has.
key_facts: Underfitting: too simple, bad on training and new data
Overfitting: learns noise, good on training but poor on new data
High bias leads to underfitting; high variance leads to overfitting
Compare training error with validation error to diagnose

questions.question: Which description matches a model with high variance?
options: It has no parameters to fit
It performs equally badly on training and test data
A slightly different training sample would produce a very different model
It assumes a straight line when the truth is curved
questions.correct_answer: A slightly different training sample would produce a very different model
questions.explanation: Variance is sensitivity to the particular training set. Wrong assumptions, like a straight line for a curve, are bias.
questions.evidence_quote: Variance is the error that comes from sensitivity to the particular training set

questions.question: Training error and validation error are both high and close together. What should you try?
options: Stronger regularisation
Stop training earlier
More features or a more flexible model
Fewer features
questions.correct_answer: More features or a more flexible model
questions.explanation: High, similar errors mean the model is underfitting. It needs more capacity, not less.
questions.evidence_quote: If both are high and close together, the model is underfitting, so try more features or a more flexible model.

questions.question: What are the three components of expected test error in the bias-variance decomposition?
options: Training error, validation error and test error
Variance, inertia and the silhouette score
Bias, learning rate and number of epochs
Squared bias, variance and irreducible noise
questions.correct_answer: Squared bias, variance and irreducible noise
questions.explanation: Even a perfect model cannot remove the noise term, which is why test error never reaches zero on noisy data.
questions.evidence_quote: The expected test error is the sum of squared bias, variance and the irreducible noise in the data.

questions.question: Describe what it means for a model to overfit.
questions.correct_answer: The model is so flexible it learns the random noise in the training set, so it scores well on training data but poorly on unseen data.
questions.explanation: Overfitting is memorising noise instead of the underlying pattern.
questions.evidence_quote: A model overfits when it is so flexible that it also learns the random noise in the training set.

concepts.name: Regularisation and cross-validation
concepts.description: Penalising large weights with ridge (L2) and lasso (L1), tuning hyperparameters on a validation set, and k-fold cross-validation.
key_facts: Regularisation adds a penalty on large weights to the loss
Ridge (L2) shrinks weights but rarely to exactly zero
Lasso (L1) can set weights exactly to zero, giving feature selection
Tune hyperparameters on validation data, never on the test set

questions.question: Which regularisation method can remove features from the model entirely?
options: Lasso (L1), because it can drive some weights to exactly zero
Ridge (L2), because it squares the weights
Both equally, whenever lambda is positive
Neither; regularisation never changes which features are used
questions.correct_answer: Lasso (L1), because it can drive some weights to exactly zero
questions.explanation: The L1 penalty pushes small weights all the way to zero. Ridge shrinks them but rarely to exactly zero.
questions.evidence_quote: Its penalty can drive some weights to exactly zero, which removes those features from the model entirely.

questions.question: What happens when the regularisation strength lambda is set very large?
options: Every weight is pushed towards zero and the model underfits
The training loss reaches zero
The model overfits more
Regularisation is switched off
questions.correct_answer: Every weight is pushed towards zero and the model underfits
questions.explanation: A huge penalty makes small weights the only priority, so the model can no longer fit the data.
questions.evidence_quote: a very large lambda pushes every weight towards zero and causes underfitting

questions.question: Why should hyperparameters not be tuned on the test set?
options: It makes training slower
The test score would stop being an honest estimate of performance on new data
The test set is too small to train on
Hyperparameters only affect the training loss
questions.correct_answer: The test score would stop being an honest estimate of performance on new data
questions.explanation: Choosing settings by test score quietly fits them to the test set, so the score becomes optimistic.
questions.evidence_quote: must not be tuned on the test set, or the test score stops being an honest estimate

questions.question: Explain how k-fold cross-validation works.
questions.correct_answer: Split the training data into k equal parts. Train k times, each time holding out a different part for validation and training on the rest, then average the k validation scores.
questions.explanation: Every example is used for validation exactly once, which gives a more reliable estimate on small datasets.
questions.evidence_quote: The model is trained k times, each time holding out a different part for validation and training on the rest.

concepts.name: k-means clustering
concepts.description: Unsupervised grouping by alternating nearest-centroid assignment and centroid updates to minimise within-cluster sum of squares.
key_facts: Clustering is unsupervised: there are no labels
Assignment step: each point goes to its nearest centroid
Update step: each centroid moves to the mean of its points
Result depends on initialisation; k-means++ spreads starting centroids

questions.question: What happens in the update step of k-means?
options: The two closest clusters are merged
Each centroid moves to the mean of the points assigned to it
A new cluster is added
Each point moves to its nearest centroid
questions.correct_answer: Each centroid moves to the mean of the points assigned to it
questions.explanation: Assignment moves points between clusters; the update step moves the centroids.
questions.evidence_quote: In the update step, each centroid is moved to the mean of the points now assigned to it.

questions.question: Which quantity does k-means minimise?
options: The distance between centroids
The number of clusters
The silhouette score
The within-cluster sum of squared distances to each point's centroid (inertia)
questions.correct_answer: The within-cluster sum of squared distances to each point's centroid (inertia)
questions.explanation: Lower inertia means points sit closer to their own centroid, so clusters are tighter.
questions.evidence_quote: K-means minimises the within-cluster sum of squares, also called inertia.

questions.question: How does k-means++ improve on plain random initialisation?
options: It spreads the starting centroids far apart
It removes outliers before clustering
It chooses k automatically
It guarantees the global minimum
questions.correct_answer: It spreads the starting centroids far apart
questions.explanation: Well-separated starting centroids make it less likely that two centroids share one natural group.
questions.evidence_quote: use the k-means++ initialisation, which spreads the starting centroids far apart

questions.question: What shapes of cluster does k-means handle badly, and why?
questions.correct_answer: Elongated or nested clusters, because k-means assumes round clusters of similar size and relies on distance to a single centre.
questions.explanation: One centre per cluster only describes compact, roughly spherical groups well.
questions.evidence_quote: K-means assumes clusters are roughly round and similar in size, because it relies on distance to a single centre.

concepts.name: Choosing k and evaluating clusters
concepts.description: Why inertia alone cannot pick k, the elbow method, the silhouette score, and using domain knowledge.
key_facts: Inertia always decreases as k increases
Elbow method: pick k where the inertia curve bends
Silhouette ranges from -1 to 1; near 1 means well inside its cluster
Domain usefulness can outweigh the metric

questions.question: Why can't you choose k by picking the value with the lowest inertia?
options: Inertia is undefined for k greater than 2
Inertia always goes down as k increases, so you would always pick the largest k
Inertia ignores the distance between points
Inertia increases with k
questions.correct_answer: Inertia always goes down as k increases, so you would always pick the largest k
questions.explanation: More centroids always let points sit closer to one. With one cluster per point, inertia is zero.
questions.evidence_quote: Inertia always goes down as k increases, because more centroids mean every point can sit closer to one.

questions.question: A point has a negative silhouette score. What does that suggest?
options: The value of k is too small
It sits right at the centre of its cluster
It is exactly on the boundary between two clusters
It may be assigned to the wrong cluster
questions.correct_answer: It may be assigned to the wrong cluster
questions.explanation: Negative means the point is, on average, closer to the next cluster than to its own.
questions.evidence_quote: a negative score suggests it may be in the wrong cluster

questions.question: In the elbow method, why does the inertia curve flatten after a certain k?
options: Inertia starts to increase
Extra clusters only split groups that already belong together
The silhouette score becomes negative
The algorithm stops converging
questions.correct_answer: Extra clusters only split groups that already belong together
questions.explanation: Once each real group has a centroid, more clusters give only small gains.
questions.evidence_quote: After a point the curve flattens, because extra clusters only split groups that already belong together.

questions.question: Why might a team choose four clusters even when a metric prefers eleven?
questions.correct_answer: Because domain knowledge matters: if the team can act on four segments but not eleven, four clusters are more useful for the task.
questions.explanation: Metrics guide the choice, but the clusters have to be useful.
questions.evidence_quote: If a marketing team can act on four customer segments but not on eleven, four may be the right answer even if a metric prefers eleven.
